s.line: Our little party of travelers awakened the next morning refreshed and full of hope,
s.note: הִתְעוֹרֵר (hitpa'el) = to wake up. עוֹרֵר = to arouse or stir up, and הֵעִיר (hif'il) = to wake someone else: הָרַעַשׁ הֵעִיר אוֹתִי (the noise woke me). לְמָחֳרַת = "on the next day"; לְמָחֳרַת בַּבֹּקֶר = the next morning. Compare מָחָר = tomorrow.

s.line: and Dorothy breakfasted like a princess off peaches and plums from the trees beside the river.
s.note: שְׂפַת הַנָּהָר = the riverbank; שָׂפָה means "lip", "edge" and also "language" (שְׂפַת הַיָּם = the seashore, הַשָּׂפָה הָעִבְרִית = the Hebrew language). שֶׁעַל = "that (is) on": Hebrew often skips the verb "to be" after שֶׁ.

w: לֹא מְעַט|quite a few|~lit. not a few
s.line: Behind them was the dark forest they had passed safely through, although they had suffered many discouragements;
s.note: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁ = although; in speech you will hear the shorter אַף שֶׁ or לַמְרוֹת שֶׁ. לֹא מְעַט ("not a few") is a very common understatement for "quite a lot": יֵשׁ לִי לֹא מְעַט עֲבוֹדָה.

w: וּשְׁטוּפַת שֶׁמֶשׁ|and sunny|~lit. washed with sun
s.line: but before them was a lovely, sunny country that seemed to beckon them on to the Emerald City.
s.note: הִשְׂתָּרְעָה: in hitpa'el, when the root starts with ס, שׂ or שׁ, the ת of the prefix swaps places with it: הִשְׂתָּרֵעַ, not "hit-sara". The same happens in הִסְתַּכֵּל (to look). שְׁטוּף שֶׁמֶשׁ ("washed with sun") is a standard phrase for "sunny", common in travel ads.

s.line: To be sure, the broad river now cut them off from this beautiful land.
s.note: אָמְנָם = "true, …; admittedly", and it usually sets up an אֲבָל in the next sentence, exactly as here. בֵּין … לְבֵין = "between … and": בֵּין תֵּל אָבִיב לְבֵין חֵיפָה.

s.line: But the raft was nearly done,

w: לָצֵאת לַדֶּרֶךְ|to set out|~lit. to go out to the road
s.line: and after the Tin Woodman had cut a few more logs and fastened them together with wooden pins, they were ready to start.
s.note: מוּכָן = ready. In form it is a hof'al participle, "made ready, prepared", the passive of הֵכִין (to prepare). לָצֵאת לַדֶּרֶךְ = to set off on a journey. חִבֵּר = to join together; also "to write (a book)" and "to add (numbers)": חִבּוּר = addition.

s.line: Dorothy sat down in the middle of the raft and held Toto in her arms.
When the Cowardly Lion stepped upon the raft it tipped badly, for he was big and heavy;
s.note: הִיא refers to הָרַפְסוֹדָה: Hebrew has no "it", so a feminine noun is "she". נָטָה = to lean or tilt; also "to tend to": הוּא נוֹטֶה לְאַחֵר (he tends to be late).

s.line: but the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman stood upon the other end to steady it,
and they had long poles in their hands to push the raft through the water.
s.note: מוֹט is masculine but its plural ends in וֹת, so the adjective stays masculine: מוֹטוֹת אֲרֻכִּים. The same with מָקוֹם → מְקוֹמוֹת רַבִּים.

s.line: They got along quite well at first,
s.note: הִתְקַדֵּם = to move forward, to make progress; קָדִימָה = forward, and הִתְקַדְּמוּת = progress. יָפֶה as an adverb means "well, nicely": הִיא שָׁרָה יָפֶה.

w: מִדֶּרֶךְ הַלְּבֵנִים הַצְּהֻבּוֹת|from the yellow brick road
s.line: but when they reached the middle of the river the swift current swept the raft downstream, farther and farther away from the road of yellow brick.
s.note: סָחַף = to sweep away (of water or wind); figuratively הַשִּׁיר סָחַף אֶת הַקָּהָל (the song swept the audience along). מוֹרַד = a downward slope; בְּמוֹרַד הַנָּהָר = downstream, בְּמוֹרַד הָרְחוֹב = down the street.

s.line: And the water grew so deep that the long poles would not touch the bottom.
s.note: נַעֲשָׂה (nif'al of עָשָׂה) here means "became", not "was done". מַיִם is always plural in Hebrew, so: הַמַּיִם נַעֲשׂוּ עֲמֻקִּים.

w: הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמַּעֲרָב|the Wicked Witch of the West
s.line: “This is bad,” said the Tin Woodman, “for if we cannot get to the land we shall be carried into the country of the Wicked Witch of the West,
s.note: נִסָּחֵף is nif'al, the passive of סָחַף (to sweep away): "we will be swept away". The נ of the future "we" form looks just like the nif'al נ, but the dagesh in ס shows this is nif'al future. יַבָּשָׁה = dry land, from יָבֵשׁ (dry).

s.line: and she will enchant us and make us her slaves.”
s.note: הָפַךְ … לְ = to turn something into something: הוּא הָפַךְ אֶת הַחֶדֶר לְמִשְׂרָד. On its own הָפַךְ = to turn over or flip. כִּשֵּׁף = to bewitch, the verb behind מְכַשֵּׁפָה.

s.line: “And then I should get no brains,” said the Scarecrow.
“And I should get no courage,” said the Cowardly Lion.
“And I should get no heart,” said the Tin Woodman.
“And I should never get back to Kansas,” said Dorothy.
s.note: לְעוֹלָם לֹא = never, about the future, a bit stronger than אַף פַּעַם לֹא. You will see it in לְעוֹלָם לֹא אֶשְׁכַּח (I will never forget). וַ in וַאֲנִי is the ordinary "and", pointed with patah before the hataf-patah of אֲנִי.

s.line: “We must certainly get to the Emerald City if we can,” the Scarecrow continued,
s.note: חַיָּב = must (literally "obliged"); it agrees like an adjective: חַיָּב, חַיֶּבֶת, חַיָּבִים. It also means "owing": אַתָּה חַיָּב לִי כֶּסֶף (you owe me money). בְּהֶחְלֵט = definitely, a very common reply: – אַתָּה בָּא? – בְּהֶחְלֵט!

s.line: and he pushed so hard on his long pole that it stuck fast in the mud at the bottom of the river.
s.note: נִתְקַע (nif'al) = to get stuck. Very common today: נִתְקַעְתִּי בַּפְּקָק (I got stuck in a traffic jam), הַמַּחְשֵׁב נִתְקַע (the computer froze). The state is the pa'ul form תָּקוּעַ, "stuck", which comes up soon.

s.line: Then, before he could pull it out again—or let go—the raft was swept away,
s.note: הִסְפִּיק = to manage (to do something) in time: לֹא הִסְפַּקְתִּי לֶאֱכֹל (I didn't get a chance to eat). It also means "to be enough": זֶה מַסְפִּיק. נִסְחֲפָה is again the nif'al passive of סָחַף.

s.line: and the poor Scarecrow was left clinging to the pole in the middle of the river.
s.note: נֶאֱחָז בְּ־ (nif'al, active meaning) = to cling to or hold on to; its pa'al אָחַז בְּ־ = to grip. Like many verbs of holding, it takes בְּ־: הֶחֱזִיק בְּ־, תָּפַס בְּ־.

w: לְהִתְרָאוֹת|goodbye|~lit. to see each other again
s.line: “Good-bye!” he called after them,
s.note: לְהִתְרָאוֹת = goodbye, literally "to see one another (again)": a hitpa'el infinitive of רָאָה, where hitpa'el gives the "each other" meaning. In speech you will also hear בַּיי and יַאלְלָה, בַּיי.

s.line: and they were very sorry to leave him.
s.note: צַר לִי = I'm sorry (about something sad): צַר לִי לִשְׁמֹעַ (I'm sorry to hear it). To apologize, say סְלִיחָה or אֲנִי מִצְטַעֵר. הִשְׁאִיר (hif'il) = to leave something behind, the causative of נִשְׁאַר (to stay).

s.line: Indeed, the Tin Woodman began to cry,
but fortunately remembered that he might rust, and so dried his tears on Dorothy’s apron.
s.note: עָלוּל = "might, is liable to", used for things you don't want to happen: עָלוּל לָרֶדֶת גֶּשֶׁם. For something good you say עָשׂוּי: הוּא עָשׂוּי לְהַצְלִיחַ. נִזְכַּר (nif'al, active meaning) = to suddenly remember, recall; זָכַר = to remember (in general).

s.line: Of course this was a bad thing for the Scarecrow.
s.note: כַּמּוּבָן = of course, literally "as (is) understood". מוּבָן is the hof'al participle of הֵבִין (to understand): זֶה לֹא מוּבָן לִי (I don't get it).

s.line: “I am now worse off than when I first met Dorothy,” he thought.
s.note: גָּרוּעַ = bad, poor in quality; גָּרוּעַ יוֹתֵר = worse, and הֲכִי גָּרוּעַ = the worst. "Worse off" becomes "my situation is worse", הַמַּצָּב שֶׁלִּי. You will hear מָה הַמַּצָּב? as "how are things?"

w: לְהַעֲמִיד פָּנִים|to pretend|~idiom: lit. to set up a face
s.line: “Then, I was stuck on a pole in a cornfield, where I could make-believe scare the crows, at any rate.
s.note: לְהַעֲמִיד פָּנִים = to pretend, a fixed phrase used all the time: הוּא מַעֲמִיד פָּנִים שֶׁהוּא יָשֵׁן (he's pretending to be asleep). מַפְחִיד = scaring (hif'il, "to make afraid"); as an adjective it means "scary": סֶרֶט מַפְחִיד.

s.line: But surely there is no use for a Scarecrow stuck on a pole in the middle of a river.
s.note: תּוֹעֶלֶת = use, benefit: אֵין בָּזֶה תּוֹעֶלֶת (it's no use). בֶּטַח = surely, probably, very common in speech; בֶּטַח! on its own = "sure!"

w: בְּסוֹפוֹ שֶׁל דָּבָר|after all|~idiom: lit. at the end of the matter
יִהְיֶה לִי|I will have|~lit. there will be to me
s.line: I am afraid I shall never have any brains, after all!”
s.note: חוֹשֵׁשׁ = to fear, to be concerned, a step more formal than פּוֹחֵד; חֲשָׁשׁ = a concern, a word you'll meet often in the news. בְּסוֹפוֹ שֶׁל דָּבָר = in the end, after all.

s.line: Down the stream the raft floated, and the poor Scarecrow was left far behind.
s.note: צָף = to float (pa'al, hollow root צ־ו־ף); the past is צָף / צָפָה. Don't confuse it with צָפָה = "watched", from the root צ־פ־ה: צָפָה בַּטֶּלֶוִיזְיָה. Without vowels the two look identical.

s.line: Then the Lion said:
“Something must be done to save us.
s.note: צָרִיךְ + infinitive with no subject = "something has to be done", the usual Hebrew way around the English passive ("must be done").

s.line: I think I can swim to the shore and pull the raft after me, if you will only hold fast to the tip of my tail.”
s.note: הֶחֱזִיק בְּ־ = to hold on to (with בְּ־), while הֶחֱזִיק אֶת = to hold something (in your hands). מָשַׁךְ = to pull; on doors in Israel you'll see מְשֹׁךְ (pull) and דְּחֹף (push).

s.line: So he sprang into the water, and the Tin Woodman caught fast hold of his tail.
Then the Lion began to swim with all his might toward the shore.
s.note: בְּכָל כּוֹחוֹ = with all his strength; בְּכָל הַכּוֹחַ is the everyday form. לְעֵבֶר = toward, a little more written than לְכִוּוּן.

s.line: It was hard work, although he was so big;

w: לְאַט לְאַט|little by little|~lit. slowly slowly
אֶל מִחוּץ לַזֶּרֶם|out of the current
s.line: but by and by they were drawn out of the current, and then Dorothy took the Tin Woodman’s long pole and helped push the raft to the land.
s.note: נִמְשְׁכוּ is nif'al, here the passive of מָשַׁךְ: "they were pulled". The same verb also means "to be drawn to" and "to last": הִיא נִמְשֶׁכֶת לְמוּזִיקָה, הַפְּגִישָׁה נִמְשְׁכָה שָׁעָה (the meeting lasted an hour).

s.line: They were all tired out when they reached the shore at last and stepped off upon the pretty green grass,
s.note: סוֹף סוֹף ("end end") = at long last, with a sense of relief: סוֹף סוֹף הִגַּעְנוּ! Plain לְבַסּוֹף = finally, in the end, without the relief. תָּשׁוּשׁ = worn out, a stronger word than עָיֵף.

w: מֵעֵבֶר לְדֶרֶךְ הַלְּבֵנִים הַצְּהֻבּוֹת|beyond the yellow brick road
s.line: and they also knew that the stream had carried them a long way past the road of yellow brick that led to the Emerald City.
s.note: מוֹבִילָה = leads (hif'il participle). The same verb means "to transport" (הוֹבָלָה = moving / haulage) and "to be in the lead": הַקְּבוּצָה מוֹבִילָה בַּטַּבְלָה.

s.line: “What shall we do now?” asked the Tin Woodman, as the Lion lay down on the grass to let the sun dry him.
s.note: כְּדֵי שֶׁ + future = "so that": כְּדֵי שֶׁהַשֶּׁמֶשׁ תְּיַבֵּשׁ אוֹתוֹ. With no new subject it is כְּדֵי + infinitive (כְּדֵי לָנוּחַ). שֶׁמֶשׁ is usually feminine, hence תְּיַבֵּשׁ.

s.line: “We must get back to the road, in some way,” said Dorothy.
s.note: אֵיכְשֶׁהוּ = somehow, from אֵיךְ + שֶׁהוּא. The same pattern gives מַשֶּׁהוּ (something), מִישֶׁהוּ (someone) and אֵיפֹשֶׁהוּ (somewhere).

s.line: “The best plan will be to walk along the riverbank until we come to the road again,” remarked the Lion.
s.note: הֵעִיר = to remark, comment (הֶעָרָה = a comment). It is spelled exactly like הֵעִיר = "woke (someone) up", from the same root ע־ו־ר; only context tells them apart. גָּדָה = riverbank; הַגָּדָה הַמַּעֲרָבִית = the West Bank.

s.line: So, when they were rested, Dorothy picked up her basket and they started along the grassy bank, to the road from which the river had carried them.
s.note: מְכֻסֶּה = covered, the pu'al participle of כִּסָּה (to cover). Notice it needs no "with": מְכֻסֶּה דֶּשֶׁא, מְכֻסֶּה שֶׁלֶג. שֶׁמִּמֶּנָּה = "from which", literally "that from her": Hebrew repeats the noun as a pronoun inside the relative clause.

w: שֶׁשִּׂמְּחוּ אֶת לִבָּם|that cheered them|~lit. that gladdened their heart
s.line: It was a lovely country, with plenty of flowers and fruit trees and sunshine to cheer them,
s.note: נֶהְדָּר = wonderful, lovely, a favorite word of praise: נֶהְדָּר! (great!). שִׂמַּח (pi'el) = to make happy, the causative-like pi'el of שָׂמַח (to be glad).

w: וְאִלְמָלֵא|and if not for (the fact that)
s.line: and had they not felt so sorry for the poor Scarecrow, they could have been very happy.
s.note: אִלְמָלֵא = "if not, were it not that", a slightly literary word you will meet in writing and news commentary; in speech you would say אִם הֵם לֹא הָיוּ מִצְטַעֲרִים. הִצְטַעֵר (hitpa'el): with צ as first letter the prefix ת swaps places and turns into ט.

s.line: They walked along as fast as they could, Dorothy only stopping once to pick a beautiful flower;
s.note: כְּכָל שֶׁ־ = "as … as (one can)": מַהֵר כְּכָל שֶׁיָּכְלוּ = as fast as they could. The everyday version is כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר מַהֵר (as fast as possible). קָטַף = to pick (flowers, fruit); קָטִיף = harvest of fruit.

s.line: and after a time the Tin Woodman cried out: “Look!”
s.note: תִּרְאוּ! = look! It is the future form used as a command, which is how most Israelis give commands in speech. The "real" imperative רְאוּ! sounds more formal. Likewise תָּבוֹא! for בּוֹא!.

s.line: Then they all looked at the river and saw the Scarecrow perched upon his pole in the middle of the water,
s.note: הִבִּיט בְּ־ = to look at, with בְּ־, like הִסְתַּכֵּל בְּ־. After a verb of seeing, a participle describes what the person was doing: רָאוּ אֶת הַדַּחְלִיל יוֹשֵׁב = they saw the Scarecrow sitting.

s.line: looking very lonely and sad.
“What can we do to save him?” asked Dorothy.

w: הֵנִיעוּ בְּרֹאשָׁם|shook their heads|~הֵנִיעַ בְּרֹאשׁוֹ = move one's head
s.line: The Lion and the Woodman both shook their heads, for they did not know.
s.note: הֵנִיעַ בְּרֹאשׁוֹ just means "moved his head", so Hebrew adds לְשָׁלִילָה (in the negative) for a "no" and לְחִיּוּב for a nodded "yes". הֵנִיעַ is the hif'il of נ־ו־ע (to move); מָנוֹעַ = an engine and הֲנָעָה = drive, as in a car's four-wheel drive.

s.line: So they sat down upon the bank and gazed wistfully at the Scarecrow until a Stork flew by, who, upon seeing them, stopped to rest at the water’s edge.
s.note: חֲסִידָה = stork. It is feminine, which suits Baum, who calls the stork "she". Storks pass over Israel in huge numbers every spring and autumn, so the word is well known. בַּסְּבִיבָה = in the area, nearby; אֵיכוּת הַסְּבִיבָה = the environment (literally "quality of the surroundings").

s.line: “Who are you and where are you going?” asked the Stork.
s.note: לְאָן = where to; אֵיפֹה = where (location); מֵאַיִן or מֵאֵיפֹה = where from. English uses one word, Hebrew needs the direction. The וּ in וּלְאָן is "and" before a shva.

s.line: “I am Dorothy,” answered the girl, “and these are my friends, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion;
and we are going to the Emerald City.”
s.note: בַּדֶּרֶךְ לְ־ = on the way to; it needs no verb. You will hear it every day: אֲנִי בַּדֶּרֶךְ (I'm on my way), בַּדֶּרֶךְ הַבַּיְתָה (on the way home).

s.line: “This isn’t the road,” said the Stork, as she twisted her long neck and looked sharply at the queer party.
s.note: זֹאת, not זֶה, because דֶּרֶךְ is feminine (though some speakers treat it as masculine). חֲבוּרָה = a group of companions, a gang of friends, from חָבֵר. סוֹבֵב = to turn something around; הִסְתּוֹבֵב = to turn (oneself) around.

s.line: “I know it,” returned Dorothy, “but we have lost the Scarecrow, and are wondering how we shall get him again.”
s.note: אִבֵּד (pi'el) = to lose something; אָבַד (pa'al) = to be lost, to get lost (of a thing): הַמַּפְתֵּחַ אָבַד. A lost person הָלַךְ לְאִבּוּד. הֶחֱזִיר (hif'il) = to bring or give back, the causative of חָזַר (to return).

s.line: “Where is he?” asked the Stork.
“Over there in the river,” answered the little girl.

w: הָיִיתִי מְבִיאָה|I would bring|hif'il ptc · ב־ו־א
s.line: “If he wasn’t so big and heavy I would get him for you,” remarked the Stork.
s.note: An unreal condition: אִלּוּ (or אִם) + הָיָה …, then הָיִיתִי + participle: הָיִיתִי מְבִיאָה = I would bring. This is the regular way to say "would" in modern Hebrew: אִם הָיָה לִי זְמַן, הָיִיתִי בָּא.

s.line: “He isn’t heavy a bit,” said Dorothy eagerly, “for he is stuffed with straw;
s.note: מְמֻלָּא = stuffed, filled, the pu'al participle of מִלֵּא (to fill). In the kitchen: פִּלְפֵּל מְמֻלָּא (stuffed pepper), and the dish מְמֻלָּאִים. בְּהִתְלַהֲבוּת = with enthusiasm; מִתְלַהֵב = excited, keen.

w: אֲסִירֵי תּוֹדָה|grateful|~idiom: lit. prisoners of thanks
s.line: and if you will bring him back to us, we shall thank you ever and ever so much.”
s.note: אֲסִיר תּוֹדָה ("a prisoner of thanks") = deeply grateful, a set phrase in polite speech and letters: אֲנִי אֲסִיר תּוֹדָה לְךָ. Here it is plural construct, אֲסִירֵי.

s.line: “Well, I’ll try,” said the Stork, “but if I find he is too heavy to carry I shall have to drop him in the river again.”
s.note: הִתְבָּרֵר (hitpa'el) = to turn out, become clear: הִתְבָּרֵר שֶׁ… = it turned out that …, constant in the news. הִצְטָרֵךְ = to have to, need to; again the hitpa'el ת turns into ט after צ. מִדַּי … מִכְּדֵי = too … to.

s.line: So the big bird flew into the air and over the water till she came to where the Scarecrow was perched upon his pole.
s.note: צִפּוֹר is feminine: הַצִּפּוֹר הַגְּדוֹלָה, צִפּוֹרִים קְטַנּוֹת. שֶׁבּוֹ = "in which, where", literally "that in it", the usual written way to say "where" after מָקוֹם; in speech, אֵיפֹה שֶׁ.

s.line: Then the Stork with her great claws grabbed the Scarecrow by the arm and carried him up into the air and back to the bank,
s.note: נָשָׂא = to carry, a little more literary than סָחַב; it also means "to marry (a woman)" in older Hebrew and "to bear" (נָשָׂא בָּאַחְרָיוּת = bore the responsibility). בַּחֲזָרָה = back (again): תַּחֲזִיר לִי אֶת זֶה בַּחֲזָרָה.

s.line: where Dorothy and the Lion and the Tin Woodman and Toto were sitting.
When the Scarecrow found himself among his friends again, he was so happy that he hugged them all, even the Lion and Toto;
s.note: מָצָא אֶת עַצְמוֹ = found himself, in the same sense as in English. עֶצֶם + possessive is the reflexive "self": אֶת עַצְמִי, אֶת עַצְמָהּ. חִבֵּק (pi'el) = to hug; חִבּוּק = a hug.

s.line: and as they walked along he sang “Tol-de-ri-de-oh!” at every step, he felt so gay.
s.note: עַלִּיז = merry, cheerful, the right word for Baum's "gay" in its old sense. Putting כָּל כָּךְ עַלִּיז first gives it weight: "so cheerful he was". שָׁר is a hollow verb: the past שָׁר and the present שָׁר look the same.

s.line: “I was afraid I should have to stay in the river forever,” he said, “but the kind Stork saved me,
s.note: לְהִשָּׁאֵר is the nif'al infinitive of נִשְׁאַר (to stay): the נ of the past disappears and the first root letter gets a dagesh. Compare לְהִכָּנֵס (to enter) from נִכְנַס.

w: יִהְיֶה לִי|I will have|~lit. there will be to me
וְאֶגְמֹל לָהּ טוֹבָה|and repay her kindness|~idiom: גָּמַל טוֹבָה = to repay a favor
s.line: and if I ever get any brains I shall find the Stork again and do her some kindness in return.”
s.note: גָּמַל טוֹבָה לְ־ = to repay someone's kindness, a set phrase. The same root gives גְּמִילוּת חֲסָדִים (acts of loving-kindness, charity). אֵי פַּעַם = ever, at any time: הָיִיתָ אֵי פַּעַם בְּאֵילַת?

w: אֵין בְּעַד מָה|you're welcome|~idiom: lit. there is nothing for which
s.line: “That’s all right,” said the Stork, who was flying along beside them.
s.note: אֵין בְּעַד מָה = "you're welcome", the standard answer to תּוֹדָה. Literally "there is nothing for which (to thank)". In speech it is often shortened to אֵין בְּעַד or replaced with בְּכֵיף (with pleasure).

s.line: “I always like to help anyone in trouble.
s.note: נִמְצָא (nif'al) = "is located, is (somewhere)", not "is found": אֵיפֹה נִמְצָא הַבַּנְק? (where is the bank?). עָזַר לְ־ takes לְ־: אֲנִי עוֹזֵר לְךָ. צָרָה = trouble; צָרוֹת in the plural is everyday for "troubles, problems".

s.line: But I must go now, for my babies are waiting in the nest for me.
s.note: גּוֹזָל = a baby bird, a chick still in the nest. חִכָּה לְ־ = to wait for: חִכִּיתִי לְךָ שָׁעָה. Compare the noun קֵן (nest) with כֵּן (yes): they sound the same but are spelled with different letters.

s.line: I hope you will find the Emerald City and that Oz will help you.”
s.note: מְקַוֶּה / מְקַוָּה = I hope (masc. / fem.), pi'el of ק־ו־ה, the same root as תִּקְוָה (hope), the name of Israel's national anthem, הַתִּקְוָה.

s.line: “Thank you,” replied Dorothy,
and then the kind Stork flew into the air and was soon out of sight.
s.note: נֶעֱלַם (nif'al, active meaning) = to disappear; נֶעְלָם as a noun = "an unknown" (in math, and figuratively). הֶעֱלִים (hif'il) = to make disappear, to hide: הַעֲלָמַת מַס = tax evasion. הִתְרוֹמֵם = to rise up, from the root of רָם (high).

s.line: They walked along listening to the singing of the brightly colored birds and looking at the lovely flowers which now became so thick that the ground was carpeted with them.
s.note: Two verbs, two prepositions: הִקְשִׁיב לְ־ = to listen to, הִסְתַּכֵּל בְּ־ = to look at. צָפוּף = dense, crowded: הָרַכֶּבֶת הָיְתָה צְפוּפָה (the train was packed).

s.line: There were big yellow and white and blue and purple blossoms, besides great clusters of scarlet poppies,
s.note: Color adjectives in the <t>קָטֹל</t> pattern double the middle letter in the plural: <t>צָהֹב → צְהֻבִּים</t>, <t>כָּחֹל → כְּחֻלִּים</t>, <t>סָגֹל → סְגֻלִּים</t>, <t>אָדֹם → אֲדֻמִּים</t>. "And" is <t>וּ</t> before a shva: <t>וּלְבָנִים, וּכְחֻלִּים</t>.

s.line: which were so brilliant in color they almost dazzled Dorothy’s eyes.
s.note: עַז = strong, intense: צֶבַע עַז (a vivid color), רוּחַ עַזָּה (a strong wind). Don't confuse it with עֵז (a goat). סִנְוֵר = to dazzle or blind with light, a four-letter root in pi'el: הָאוֹרוֹת סִנְוְרוּ אוֹתִי.

w: נָכוֹן שֶׁ|aren't|~idiom: lit. (is it) true that
s.line: “Aren’t they beautiful?” the girl asked, as she breathed in the spicy scent of the bright flowers.
s.note: נָכוֹן שֶׁ…? = "isn't it …?, aren't they …?", the natural way to ask for agreement; נָכוֹן? at the end works like "right?". שָׁאַף = to breathe in, and also "to aspire": שְׁאִיפָה = inhalation or ambition. מְתֻבָּל = seasoned, spiced, pu'al of תִּבֵּל; תַּבְלִין = a spice.

s.line: “I suppose so,” answered the Scarecrow.
s.note: אֲנִי מַנִּיחַ שֶׁכֵּן = I suppose so; שֶׁכֵּן = "that yes" and שֶׁלֹּא = "that no": אֲנִי חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁלֹּא (I don't think so). הִנִּיחַ literally means "to put down", and also "to assume": הַנָּחָה = an assumption, and also a discount!

w: כְּשֶׁיִּהְיֶה לִי|when I have|~lit. when there will be to me
יִמְצְאוּ חֵן בְּעֵינַי|will please me|~idiom: lit. find grace in my eyes
s.line: “When I have brains, I shall probably like them better.”
s.note: מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי = to be liked by, "to please" ("found grace in the eyes of"). The thing liked is the subject: הַסֶּרֶט מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינַי (I liked the film). It is as common as אָהַבְתִּי. כַּנִּרְאֶה = apparently, probably, from נִרְאֶה (seems).

w: הָיָה לִי|I had|~lit. there was to me
הָיִיתִי אוֹהֵב|I would love|pa'al ptc · א־ה־ב
s.line: “If I only had a heart, I should love them,” added the Tin Woodman.
s.note: הוֹסִיף (hif'il) = to add, both in speech ("he added") and in amounts: תּוֹסִיף מֶלַח (add salt). The noun is תּוֹסֶפֶת = an addition, a side dish, a supplement.

s.line: “I always did like flowers,” said the Lion.
“They seem so helpless and frail.
s.note: חֲסַר יֶשַׁע = helpless, a fixed phrase in writing and the news (יְלָדִים חַסְרֵי יֶשַׁע). חֲסַר + noun = "lacking …", like English "-less": חֲסַר סַבְלָנוּת (impatient), חֲסַר בַּיִת (homeless). שָׁבִיר = fragile; the sticker on a parcel says שָׁבִיר!

s.line: But there are none in the forest so bright as these.”
They now came upon more and more of the big scarlet poppies, and fewer and fewer of the other flowers;
s.note: נִתְקַל בְּ־ (nif'al) = to come across, run into; also "to trip over": נִתְקַלְתִּי בְּאֶבֶן, and figuratively נִתְקַלְנוּ בִּבְעָיָה (we ran into a problem). יוֹתֵר וְיוֹתֵר / פָּחוֹת וּפָחוֹת = more and more / fewer and fewer.

s.line: and soon they found themselves in the midst of a great meadow of poppies.
Now it is well known that when there are many of these flowers together their odor is so powerful that anyone who breathes it falls asleep,
s.note: יָדוּעַ = known, the pa'ul (passive) participle of יָדַע: יָדוּעַ שֶׁ… = it is known that …; כַּיָּדוּעַ = as is well known. A יָדוּעַ can also be a celebrity: אִישׁ יָדוּעַ.

s.line: and if the sleeper is not carried away from the scent of the flowers, he sleeps on and on forever.
s.note: Here Hebrew uses a plural verb with no subject, לֹא מַרְחִיקִים ("they don't take him away"), where English uses a passive ("is not carried away"). This is extremely common: אוֹמְרִים שֶׁ… = it is said that …, כָּאן לֹא מְעַשְּׁנִים = no smoking here.

s.line: But Dorothy did not know this, nor could she get away from the bright red flowers that were everywhere about;
s.note: הִתְרַחֵק (hitpa'el) = to move away (oneself), and הִרְחִיק (hif'il) = to move something or someone away, as in the previous sentence. Both come from רָחוֹק (far).

s.line: so presently her eyes grew heavy and she felt she must sit down to rest and to sleep.
s.note: עֵינַיִם is feminine, so the adjective is כְּבֵדוֹת. Most paired body parts are feminine: יָדַיִם, רַגְלַיִם, אָזְנַיִם.

s.line: But the Tin Woodman would not let her do this.
s.note: נָתַן לְ־ + infinitive = to let someone do something: תֵּן לִי לַחְשֹׁב (let me think), הֵם לֹא נָתְנוּ לָנוּ לְהִכָּנֵס (they didn't let us in).

w: לְדֶרֶךְ הַלְּבֵנִים הַצְּהֻבּוֹת|to the yellow brick road
s.line: “We must hurry and get back to the road of yellow brick before dark,” he said;
s.note: יַחְשִׁיךְ = it will get dark, an impersonal hif'il with no subject, like מַחְשִׁיךְ (it's getting dark) and מִתְבַּהֵר (it's clearing up). חֹשֶׁךְ = darkness, חָשׁוּךְ = dark.

s.line: and the Scarecrow agreed with him.

w: לַעֲמֹד עַל הָרַגְלַיִם|stand on her feet|~lit. to stand on the legs
s.line: So they kept walking until Dorothy could stand no longer.
s.note: כְּבָר לֹא = no longer, not anymore: הוּא כְּבָר לֹא גָּר פֹּה (he doesn't live here anymore). הִסְכִּים עִם = to agree with someone, הִסְכִּים לְ־ = to agree to something.

w: בְּעַל כָּרְחָהּ|in spite of herself|~idiom: against her will
s.line: Her eyes closed in spite of herself and she forgot where she was and fell among the poppies, fast asleep.
s.note: בְּעַל כָּרְחוֹ / כָּרְחָהּ = against his / her will, a higher-register idiom you'll meet in writing; in speech: בְּלִי לִרְצוֹת. נֶעֱצַם is the nif'al of עָצַם: the eyes "got closed", by themselves. Notice אֵיפֹה הִיא: in an indirect question Hebrew keeps the present ("where she is").

s.line: “What shall we do?” asked the Tin Woodman.
“If we leave her here she will die,” said the Lion.
s.note: After <t>אִם</t> about the future, Hebrew uses the future in both halves: <t>אִם נַשְׁאִיר … הִיא תָּמוּת</t>, where English says "if we leave … she will die".

s.line: “The smell of the flowers is killing us all.
I myself can scarcely keep my eyes open, and the dog is asleep already.”
s.note: בְּקֹשִׁי = barely, hardly, literally "with difficulty" (קָשֶׁה = hard): בְּקֹשִׁי שָׁמַעְתִּי (I could hardly hear). פָּתוּחַ = open, the pa'ul participle of פָּתַח, "opened"; it is feminine plural here to agree with עֵינַיִם.

s.line: It was true;
Toto had fallen down beside his little mistress.
s.note: גְּבִירָה = lady, mistress, an elevated word (the feminine of גְּבִיר, a rich man). In everyday Hebrew a dog's owner is הַבְּעָלִים, and a woman is addressed as גְּבֶרֶת: סְלִיחָה, גְּבֶרֶת.

s.line: But the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman, not being made of flesh, were not troubled by the scent of the flowers.
s.note: הֻטְרְדוּ is hof'al, the passive of the hif'il הִטְרִיד (to bother): זֶה מַטְרִיד אוֹתִי (it bothers me) → הוּא הֻטְרַד מִזֶּה (he was bothered by it). "By" after a passive is often מִ־. עָשׂוּי מִ־ = made of: עָשׂוּי מֵעֵץ.

w: כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר מַהֵר|as fast as possible|~idiom
s.line: “Run fast,” said the Scarecrow to the Lion, “and get out of this deadly flower bed as soon as you can.
s.note: קַטְלָנִי = deadly, lethal, a word you'll hear in the news: תְּאוּנָה קַטְלָנִית (a fatal accident). It belongs with קָטַל (to kill) and קֶטֶל (slaughter). כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר + adverb = as … as possible: כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר מַהֵר, כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר מֻקְדָּם.

s.line: We will bring the little girl with us, but if you should fall asleep you are too big to be carried.”
s.note: נִקַּח = "we will take": לָקַח drops its ל in the future (אֶקַּח, תִּקַּח, נִקַּח), much like a verb whose root starts with נ. תֵּרָדֵם is the nif'al future of נִרְדַּם; since ר can't take a dagesh, the prefix vowel lengthens instead: תֵּ, not תִּ.

s.line: So the Lion aroused himself and bounded forward as fast as he could go.
s.note: הִתְנַעֵר = to shake oneself (off), reflexive hitpa'el of נִעֵר (to shake something out, like a rug). It is also used figuratively: הִתְנַעֵר מֵאַחְרָיוּת = to shrug off responsibility. זִנֵּק = to leap, spring; also of prices: הַמְּחִירִים זִנְּקוּ (prices shot up).

s.line: In a moment he was out of sight.
“Let us make a chair with our hands and carry her,” said the Scarecrow.
s.note: בּוֹאוּ + "we" future = let's: בּוֹאוּ נֵלֵךְ (let's go). Speaking to one person: בּוֹא נַעֲשֶׂה / בּוֹאִי נַעֲשֶׂה. נִשָּׂא here is the pa'al future "we will carry". Unpointed, נשא can also be the past "he carried", or the nif'al נִשָּׂא "got married"; only context decides.

s.line: So they picked up Toto and put the dog in Dorothy’s lap,
s.note: Hebrew usually puts something "on the knees", עַל הַבִּרְכַּיִם, where English says "in the lap". The literary word for "lap, bosom" is חֵיק. הִנִּיחַ = to put down, place (hif'il of נ־ו־ח, to rest).

s.line: and then they made a chair with their hands for the seat and their arms for the arms and carried the sleeping girl between them through the flowers.
s.note: יָד is the hand and זְרוֹעַ the arm, though in speech יָד often covers both. מִשְׁעֶנֶת (plural מִשְׁעָנוֹת) = something to lean on: a backrest or an armrest, from נִשְׁעַן (to lean).

w: הָלְכוּ וְהָלְכוּ|walked on and on|pa'al · ה־ל־ך
וְהָיָה נִדְמֶה|and it seemed|nif'al ptc · ד־מ־ה
s.line: On and on they walked, and it seemed that the great carpet of deadly flowers that surrounded them would never end.
s.note: Repeating the verb, הָלְכוּ וְהָלְכוּ, gives "on and on": הוּא דִּבֵּר וְדִבֵּר (he talked and talked). נִדְמֶה = it seems, a bit more literary than נִרְאֶה: נִדְמֶה לִי שֶׁ… = I have a feeling that …. נִגְמַר (nif'al) = to end, run out: הֶחָלָב נִגְמַר (we're out of milk).

s.line: They followed the bend of the river, and at last came upon their friend the Lion, lying fast asleep among the poppies.
s.note: בְּעִקְבוֹת = following, in the footsteps of (עָקֵב = heel); in the news it means "in the wake of, following": בְּעִקְבוֹת הַסּוּפָה (following the storm). עִקּוּל = a bend or curve in a road or river.

s.line: The flowers had been too strong for the huge beast and he had given up at last,
s.note: נִכְנַע (nif'al, active meaning) = to give in, surrender; כְּנִיעָה = surrender. חַיָּה (animal) is feminine even when the animal is a male lion, so its adjective is עֲנָקִית, but the pronoun goes back to הוּא.

s.line: and fallen only a short distance from the end of the poppy bed, where the sweet grass spread in beautiful green fields before them.
“We can do nothing for him,” said the Tin Woodman, sadly; “for he is much too heavy to lift.
s.note: יוֹתֵר מִדַּי = too (much), a common variant of plain מִדַּי: זֶה יָקָר יוֹתֵר מִדַּי. הַרְבֵּה יוֹתֵר מִדַּי = much too.

w: עָלֵינוּ|we must|~עַל + pronoun = it is upon (us)
s.line: We must leave him here to sleep on forever, and perhaps he will dream that he has found courage at last.”
s.note: עָלֵינוּ + infinitive = "we must", literally "(it is) upon us"; a little more formal than אֲנַחְנוּ חַיָּבִים. עָלֶיךָ לְהַחְלִיט = it's up to you to decide. חָלַם = to dream; חֲלוֹם = a dream.

s.line: “I’m sorry,” said the Scarecrow.
“The Lion was a very good comrade for one so cowardly.
s.note: פַּחְדָּן = a coward, from פַּחַד (fear). The ־ָן ending marks a person with a habit or trait: שַׁקְרָן (a liar), בַּיְשָׁן (a shy person), קַמְצָן (a miser).

s.line: But let us go on.”
They carried the sleeping girl to a pretty spot beside the river, far enough from the poppy field to prevent her breathing any more of the poison of the flowers,
s.note: מַסְפִּיק = enough, the hif'il participle of הִסְפִּיק (which we saw meaning "to manage in time"). It comes after the adjective: רָחוֹק מַסְפִּיק (far enough), גָּדוֹל מַסְפִּיק. רַעַל = poison; הַרְעָלָה = poisoning, רַעִיל = poisonous.

s.line: and here they laid her gently on the soft grass and waited for the fresh breeze to waken her.
s.note: הִשְׁכִּיב (hif'il) = to lay someone down, the causative of שָׁכַב (to lie); a parent מַשְׁכִּיב אֶת הַיְּלָדִים לִישֹׁן (puts the kids to bed). In the same way תָּעִיר (hif'il, "will wake someone") is the causative partner of הִתְעוֹרֵר (to wake up). רוּחַ = wind, and here it is feminine, הָרוּחַ הָרַעֲנַנָּה.
